rows.evidence: Main article PDF p.10-11 Table 3 (rendered and read, rotated table), including adjusted mean difference and SMD columns and footnote d.
rows.rationale: Pain severity 12 mo, painTRAINER vs usual care plus: printed SMD -0.25 (-0.24 to 0.01), adjusted MD -0.4 (-0.6 to -0.2). Finding: estimate lies outside its CI, and the SMD CI includes 0 while the MD CI excludes 0. Recomputed checks in Python on transcribed Table 3 values (estimate within interval, endpoint order, sign agreement between SMD and the adjusted mean difference, and agreement of 'excludes 0' between the two intervals). Across Table 3 the SMD intervals are systematically corrupted: many are reversed, several exclude their own point estimate, some SMDs have the opposite sign from the corresponding mean difference (e.g., physical function 3-mo health coach MD 0.7 vs SMD -0.02), and several SMD intervals disagree with the MD interval on whether 0 is excluded. SMD is defined (Methods) as adjusted MD divided by the usual-care SD of change, so its interval must share the MD interval's sign pattern. This is a confirmed reporting error. I judged it substantive because SMDs with CIs are exactly what meta-analysts extract, and the printed intervals cannot be used; the MD columns and the primary outcome are unaffected.

rows.rationale: Verified wording. Mislabeling the composite summary could mislead about scale, but it is a supplementary sensitivity estimand, consistently null, and the table defines it as a win ratio. Minor.

rows.R: Any stroke 69 vs 64, rate ratio 1.08: abstract 95% CI 0.76-1.53; Figure 4B 0.77-1.51. A crude Poisson interval from the counts, 1.078 x exp(+/-1.96 x sqrt(1/69+1/64)), gives 0.77-1.51, matching the figure. Abstract endpoints slightly off; inference unchanged.
rows.evidence: Main article PDF p.1 abstract and p.7 Figure 4B (rendered); text search found no other occurrence of the CI.
rows.rationale: Python: RR=69/64=1.078; SE(log)=sqrt(1/69+1/64)=0.175; CI 0.767-1.515, which rounds to 0.77-1.51 (equal follow-up approximation). The abstract interval is about 4% wider on the log scale. Small discrepancy in an exploratory outcome; minor.

rows.R: Excluded: Figure 4B patch arm shows presumed ischemic 60 + hemorrhagic 12 = 72 vs any stroke 69. Rows are participant-level time-to-first-event outcomes (percentages use n=2520), so a participant with both stroke types counts in each subtype row but once in 'any stroke'. Three such participants is plausible; rows are not presented as a partition.
rows.evidence: Main article PDF p.7 Figure 4B and caption (rendered).
rows.rationale: 60/2520=2.4%, 12/2520=0.5%, 69/2520=2.7%, so counts are participants with at least one event of each type, analyzed separately as time-to-event outcomes per the caption. Under that standard convention subtype counts need not sum to the composite; the usual-care equality (58+6=64) simply reflects no overlap. A footnote would help, but this is a satisfactory explanation rather than an error. I disagreed with the AI suggestion to retain.

rows.R: Excluded: text P=.78 for day-60 deaths 28/101 vs 26/104 is a fixed-time 2x2 test; Methods state categorical outcomes used chi-square/Fisher tests (R). Yates-corrected chi-square gives P=0.776 (.78). eFigure 2's P=0.56 is explicitly a log-rank test of time to death. Different, labeled tests; no conflict.
rows.evidence: Main article PDF p.1 abstract, p.3-4 Statistical Analysis (chi-square/Fisher for categorical, log-rank for censored; R 4.4.2), p.4 Secondary Outcomes; supp3 PDF p.11 eFigure 2 (rendered).
rows.rationale: Python/scipy on [[28,73],[26,78]]: Yates chi-square P=0.776, uncorrected chi-square P=0.658, Fisher P=0.751. The .78 reproduces R's default chisq.test (Yates correction) for a categorical outcome, consistent with the stated methods, while 0.56 is labeled log-rank in the figure. Both are valid analyses of different formulations of the endpoint. The text could name the test, but this is not an inconsistency. I disagreed with the AI suggestion to retain.

rows.R: eTable 4 abbreviation list defines 'RR = risk difference', but the table header and the methods note in the same footnote say binary outcomes report relative risks from robust Poisson regression, and the estimates are ratios (e.g., 0.86). Copyediting error; meaning clear from context.
rows.evidence: Supp4 (results eAppendix) PDF p.8 eTable 4 footnotes (rendered); p.7 header per candidate evidence.

rows.R: Excluded: protocol (p.4) prints eligibility 22 0/7 - 28 6/7 weeks, as does the article (22 weeks 0 days to 28 weeks 6 days). No discrepancy; the earlier '27 6/7' was an extraction error.

rows.R: Excluded: the 2020 manual lists GMFCS 3-5 only as 'an example of such a definition', stating severe NDI will use the definition agreed at the first follow-up (BSID-IV transition). SAP v1.3 (2024) fixes GMFCS 4-5. The manual anticipates the later definition, so no conflict; 2-year outcomes are not reported here.

An example ... could be ... GMFCS level 3-5'). The SAP is the later, governing specification. Different wording in a provisional example is not a planning-material inconsistency. I disagreed with the AI suggestion to retain.

rows.R: Excluded: manual and SAP both specify BSID-IV (fourth edition) cognitive composite <70; no Bayley-III wording on the cited pages.

rows.R: Excluded: protocol p.29 and SAP p.26 (page 19 of SAP) both print efficacy alpha 0.000015 at 25%, 0.0030 at 50%, 0.0183 at 75%, 0.0440 final. No mismatch.
rows.evidence: Protocol supp1 PDF p.29 section 5.5.2.2 and SAP supp3 PDF p.26 section 7.4.2 (both rendered).
rows.rationale: Verified identical values. Agree with AI exclusion.

rows.R: Excluded: SAP 7.4.2 states the final-analysis alpha 'will depend on if/when the prior analyses have taken place' and unspent alpha from skipped looks 'may be recovered'. Trial stopped for futility at 50% (75% look not done), so a final alpha of .049 rather than the nominal .0440 is consistent with the plan. Primary RR 1.00 (0.90-1.11), so immaterial.
rows.evidence: SAP supp3 PDF p.26 (rendered); protocol supp1 PDF p.29 (rendered); main article PDF p.3 Statistical Analysis and p.1 abstract (text).
rows.rationale: Lan-DeMets O'Brien-Fleming check in Python (scipy, multivariate normal): with looks at 25% and 50% and a final look at reduced information (t=0.55-0.60) spending the remaining alpha, the final nominal level is about 0.0498-0.05; at full information with only 2 interims it is 0.0478. So recovering unspent alpha yields values near .049, as the SAP allows. I could not reproduce .049 exactly because actual information fractions are not reported, but the difference follows the plan's own rule and cannot affect the null primary result. I disagreed with the AI suggestion to retain.

rows.R: Excluded: protocol and SAP say 'Given that there are 15 centers in the NRN' when discussing site adjustment; that describes network size at the time, not a planned or capped site count. The article reports 17 participating NRN centers. Not a planned-versus-reported change in conduct.
rows.evidence: Protocol supp1 PDF p.29 (rendered); SAP supp3 PDF p.26 (rendered, same sentence); main article PDF p.1 and p.4 (17 centers).
rows.rationale: Read the context of '15 centers' in both plan documents: it explains why site adjustment might be infeasible, not an eligibility or recruitment specification. Network membership changes across funding cycles. No meaningful protocol-report difference. I disagreed with the AI suggestion to retain.

rows.R: Excluded: Table 3 RR 0.69 (0.33-1.46) for 13/312 vs 18/299 is footnoted (g) as an RR estimated by Mantel-Haenszel methods approximated by the common OR after Poisson nonconvergence, as the Methods state. With 4-6% risks OR approximates RR (crude RR 0.692, crude OR 0.679). Transparent labeling, not a conflict.
rows.evidence: Main article PDF p.8 Table 3 and footnote g (rendered); p.3 Statistical Analysis (text).
rows.rationale: Python: crude RR=(13/312)/(18/299)=0.692; crude OR=0.679. Methods: 'For models with convergence or fit issues, the RR was estimated by the Mantel-Haenszel common odds ratio'. The column header itself says 'Relative risk or odds ratio'. The label and footnote are consistent descriptions of target and estimator. I disagreed with the AI suggestion to retain.

rows.R: Excluded: eTable 3 header 'Relative Risk (95% CI)' with footnote b stating that for sparse rows RR 'was approximated by the crude (unadjusted) odds ratio with exact 95% CI'. Printed values match crude ORs (e.g., 3/322 vs 4/313 gives OR 0.726, printed 0.73). Disclosed approximation, consistent with Methods.
rows.evidence: Supp4 PDF p.5-6 eTable 3 and footnotes b and e (rendered).
rows.rationale: Python: OR for 3/322 vs 4/313 = 0.726 (printed 0.73); 2/322 vs 3/313 = 0.646 (0.65); SAE hyperglycemia 8/322 vs 3/313 = 2.63 (2.64), confirming the footnoted estimator. With these low risks OR approximates RR. Header plus footnote is a transparent, compatible description. I disagreed with the AI suggestion to retain.

rows.R: Protocol 3.2: primary endpoint = 1 if at least one of >=5% weight loss, >=4% loss plus >=150 min/wk activity, or >=0.2% A1C reduction. Article: composite achieved only among participants who maintained A1C <6.5% throughout; supplement says diabetes-range A1C at 6/12 mo counted as failure regardless of other components. Primary endpoint definition differs.
rows.evidence: Protocol supp1 PDF p.15 section 3.2 (rendered; custom-encoded text); main article PDF p.1 abstract and p.4 Primary Analysis (text); supp2 PDF p.29-30 eTable 13 description (text).
rows.rationale: Verified both definitions. The protocol notes that analyses may be aligned with updated CDC benchmarks, but the supplied protocol does not specify the A1C <6.5% condition and no amendment is supplied. Adding a failure condition to a noninferiority primary endpoint is a substantive endpoint-definition difference, although with 4.4% vs 3.8% diabetes-range A1C its numerical impact is probably small.

rows.R: Supplement A1C device table, 12-month column: Afinion 282 + A1CNow+ 30 + serum 0 = 312, but 313 participants completed with complete outcomes (main text). Baseline column sums to 368. The text names a Siemens DCA Vantage device not listed in the table, a likely source of the missing 1.
rows.evidence: Supp2 PDF p.8 A1C Measurement table (text); main article PDF p.4 (313 completers).
rows.rationale: Arithmetic: 282+30+0=312 vs 313; baseline 334+33+1=368 matches randomized N. The follow-up row therefore omits one measurement, probably on an unlisted device. Real but trivial reconciliation gap; no effect on outcomes.

rows.R: Figure 3 footnote: 'Baseline median (IQR) weight: 32.2 (28.2-35.9) kg/m2 ... 32.5 (29.3-37.7)'; these are the Table 1 BMI values and the unit is kg/m2. Label should be BMI; intended meaning recoverable.
rows.evidence: Main article PDF p.8 Figure 3 footnote a and PDF p.6 Table 1 BMI row (text extraction, values matched).
rows.rationale: Matched identical triplets in Table 1 BMI row and the figure footnote. Mislabel only; minor.

rows.R: Footnote 'Age differed between study groups (p = 0.014); all other baseline characteristics were similar' is repeated under eTables 5-7, which compare sites, A1C strata and completers vs dropouts. It refers to the randomized arms (main Table 1 P=.01), but in eTable 7 it sits beside a note that no characteristics differed. Confusing copied footnote.
rows.evidence: Supp2 PDF p.39-47 eTables 3, 5, 6, 7 footnotes (text extracted and read); main article PDF p.6 Table 1.
rows.rationale: Read each footnote. eTable 5 separately reports site-age p=0.017; eTable 7 footnote 1 says no characteristic differed while footnote 2 says age differed, which only makes sense if footnote 2 concerns the randomized arms. Real presentation problem with no effect on results; minor.

rows.R: Excluded: eTable 7 footnote 'No baseline characteristics were statistically significant different between groups (p<0.05)' uses the parenthesis to state the significance threshold, a common shorthand, not a claim that p<0.05. The apparent conflict with the age note is the copied-footnote problem already retained as C004.
rows.evidence: Supp2 PDF p.47 eTable 7 footnotes 1-2 (text).
rows.rationale: Read the wording; '(p<0.05)' as the criterion for significance is a conventional, if loose, phrasing. No numerical or statistical error beyond C004. I disagreed with the AI suggestion to retain.

rows.R: Prohibited medications 6/183 vs 7/185, P=.793: eTable 10 methods say chi-squared; eTable 10b footnote says Wilcoxon rank-sum. Recomputed: uncorrected chi-square P=0.7930, Wilcoxon on the binary indicator P=0.7933; both give .793, so only the test label conflicts.
rows.evidence: Supp2 PDF p.29 (eTable 10 method description) and p.52 eTable 10b (text).
rows.rationale: scipy: chi2_contingency without correction P=0.79299; Mann-Whitney without continuity P=0.79326 (Yates and Fisher give 1.0). The P value is reproducible under either label, so the issue is the inconsistent test name only. Minor.

rows.R: eTable 16 MI sensitivity: pooled AI 32.2%, human 31.9%, but AI-minus-human RD -1.1 points (1-sided lower bound -11.5). 32.2-31.9=+0.3, so sign and size conflict; human 31.9% also equals the unimputed 59/185. Which value is wrong cannot be determined; noninferiority (margin -15) would hold either way.
rows.evidence: Supp2 PDF p.30 (eTable 16 method) and p.59 eTable 16 (text); main article PDF p.1 and p.4 primary result 31.7% vs 31.9%, RD -0.2.
rows.rationale: 32.2-31.9=0.3, not -1.1; even an adjusted RD would not usually reverse sign relative to marginal pooled percentages this close. The human-arm pooled value identical to the complete-case-as-failure proportion (59/185=31.9%) suggests a transcription error. The sensitivity-analysis effect estimate is therefore unusable for extraction; I rated it substantive for that reason, while noting the noninferiority conclusion is not threatened.

rows.R: Table 2, continuous abstinence self-reported (ITT): adjusted RR 2.8 (1.9 to 42); crude 2.7 (1.8 to 4.1). On the log scale 2.8 with lower 1.9 implies an upper limit near 4.1, so '42' is almost certainly 4.2 with a dropped decimal. Obvious typo, but an extractor could copy 42.
rows.evidence: Main article PDF p.6 Table 2 (rendered).
rows.rationale: Python: ln(2.8)-ln(1.9)=0.388; ln(2.8)+0.388 gives exp=4.13. A Wald-type interval for a log RR is symmetric on the log scale, so an upper limit of 42 is incompatible with 2.8 and 1.9. Confirmed typographic error; the intended value is recoverable and inference is unchanged. Minor, with possible extraction impact.

rows.R: Discussion: '4.8% of the trial participants died of TB within 6 months'. 4.8% is all-cause mortality (25+27=52/1080; Results say '4.8% had died'). eTable 4 attributes 32/52 deaths to TB, i.e., 32/1080=3.0%. TB-specific mortality is overstated by about 60%.
rows.evidence: Main article PDF p.5 Results (4.8% had died), p.6 Table 2 death rows, p.8 Discussion (text); supp2 PDF p.6 eTable 4 (text).
rows.rationale: Python: 52/1080=4.81%; 32/1080=2.96%. The Discussion attributes all deaths to TB and uses that to compare with another trial's death rate. A quantitative cause-specific claim is wrong by a factor of 1.6, which could mislead readers about TB mortality in this population; I rated it substantive although it sits in the Discussion and is labeled exploratory.

rows.R: Protocol V6.0 p.16: 'a total of 178 SMS messages over 6 months', with 4-5/day for 2 months, 2-3/day for 2 months, 1-2/week for 2 months. The schedule's minimum is about 60x4+60x2+9=369 messages, so the total and the schedule cannot both hold. The delivered regimen in the article (134 = 100+30+4) follows a different schedule.
rows.evidence: Supp1 (protocol compilation) PDF p.16 lines 386-390 (rendered); main article PDF p.3 (text).
rows.rationale: Arithmetic in Python as stated. A 'unique message' versus 'send' distinction could reconcile part of it, but the text says each participant 'will receive a total of 178'. Internal plan inconsistency in intervention-dose description. Because the article clearly describes what was delivered, I rated it minor for understanding the reported trial.

rows.R: Protocol V6.0 gives the same 2,384-participant plan as '~50 recruits from 44 health facilities' (p.10) and '~50 recruits from 48 health clinics' (p.26). 2384/50=47.7, consistent with 48; 44 x 50=2200. Internal inconsistency in the cluster count; this plan was superseded by the 27-cluster phase 3 actually run.
rows.evidence: Supp1 PDF p.10 section 4.2 and p.26 section 11.1 (rendered).
rows.rationale: Verified both passages; all other parameters identical. 44 appears to be the error. Plan text only; the reported trial used 27 clusters. Minor.

rows.R: Protocol (p.53): 'a total of 134 SMS messages over 6 months', 4-5/day for 2 months, 1-2/day for 2 months, 1/week for 2 months; minimum about 60x4+60x1+8=308. Total and schedule conflict. Another plan document (p.80) gives 134 with 3-4/day for 1 month, 1/day for 1 month, 1/month for 4 months (124-154), matching the article.
rows.evidence: Supp1 PDF p.53 lines 1527-1530 and p.80 lines 2533-2536 (rendered); main article PDF p.3.
rows.rationale: Arithmetic in Python: p.53 minimum 308 vs 134; p.80 range 124-154 contains 134; article 100+30+4=134. The p.53 schedule is a carry-over inconsistent with its own total; the correct schedule is documented elsewhere. Minor.

rows.R: Protocol schedule table: 'TAM questionnaire (30% of participants in the mTB-Tobacco groups)'; text below says 20%, and the table computes 20% in phase 3 (80, 64) but 100% in phase 4 (11x45=495, 7x45=315). Three different sampling fractions for an ancillary questionnaire.
rows.evidence: Supp1 PDF p.55 (rendered).
rows.rationale: Verified header, narrative and computations: 10x40x0.2=80, 8x40x0.2=64, 11x45=495, 7x45=315. Real inconsistency in an ancillary acceptability measure; no bearing on trial outcomes. Minor.

rows.R: Same protocol version: p.48 gives 2,716 participants, ~43 recruits from 63 facilities (63x43=2709); p.62 gives 2,716 with ~50 recruits from 48 clinics (48x50=2400). The 48/~50 text is a carry-over from the earlier 2,384 plan.
rows.evidence: Supp1 PDF p.48 section 21.2 and p.62 section 28.1 (rendered); pp.51-52 diagram not inspected.
rows.rationale: Python: 63x43=2709 is close to 2716; 48x50=2400 is not. The phase 3/4 diagrams on pp.63-64 (27 and 36 sites, total 63) support 63. Carry-over text error; correct design recoverable. Minor.

rows.R: Phase 4: 1036 x 1.56 = 1616.2, printed '= 1620 (45 per site)'; 1620 = 36 x 45 after rounding up per site, a step not stated. 'Effective sample size' is also misused (ESS is n/DE, not n x DE). The DE uses m=29, while the final 45/site implies DE 1.88. Phase 4 is not part of this report.
rows.evidence: Supp1 PDF p.64 (rendered).
rows.rationale: Python: 1036*1.56=1616.16; 1616.16/36=44.9, rounded to 45, gives 1620. The arithmetic slip itself is a rounding-up step. A deeper inconsistency is that the design effect is computed with the pre-inflation cluster size (29) rather than the planned 45 (DE 1.88, n=1948). That matters for phase 4 power, but phase 4 results are not reported here, so I rated it minor for this report.

rows.R: Phase 4 noninferiority section (p.64) diagram box reads 'Total clusters in Phase 3 (Superiority trial) = 36 sites'; the surrounding text and numbers (36 sites, 1620, A vs face-to-face) are phase 4. Copy-paste label error.
rows.evidence: Supp1 PDF p.64 (rendered).
rows.rationale: Verified. Phase 3 has 27 sites (p.63), so the label is clearly a carry-over. Minor.

rows.R: Phase 3 plan: N=704, m=704/27=26, DE=1+0.02(26-1)=1.50, 'ESS'=704x1.50 'approx 1080 (40/site)'. 704x1.5=1056, rounded to 40/site. More importantly, DE is computed at m=26 but the plan recruits 40/site, where DE=1.78 (704x1.78=1253). The calculation is internally inconsistent and understates the required size.
rows.evidence: Supp1 PDF p.63 (rendered) and p.83 summary (rendered).
rows.rationale: Python: 704*1.5=1056; 1056/27=39.1, rounded to 40, gives 1080. 'Effective sample size' is misnamed (ESS = n/DE). With 40 per cluster, DE=1+0.02*39=1.78 and the inflated requirement is about 1253 (46/site); solving 704(1+0.02(m-1))=27m gives m of about 53. The plan's cluster size and design effect are mutually inconsistent, so the phase 3 sample size (the trial reported here) is smaller than its own assumptions require. I rated this substantive for the plan, although the observed effect (RR about 3) makes the power shortfall moot in hindsight.

rows.R: Plan describes MPSS as five domains on a 5-point scale 'summated to give an overall score ranging from 5 to 35'. Five 1-5 items give 5-25. Range or item description is wrong; no scoring rule given.
rows.evidence: Supp1 PDF p.85 lines 2704-2709 (rendered).
rows.rationale: Arithmetic: 5x1=5, 5x5=25. A 35 maximum would need 7 items or a different scale; the text does not say so. I did not verify the original instrument's structure. Secondary-measure description; minor.

rows.R: eTable 6: site 2008 '5 (7.5)' deaths; every site has 40 participants (eTable 5) and all other rows use /40. 5/40=12.5%. Count is right (control-site deaths sum to 27, matching Table 2); percentage is wrong.
rows.evidence: Supp2 PDF p.8 eTable 5 and p.9 eTable 6 (text).
rows.rationale: Python: 5/40=0.125. Summed control-site deaths 1+0+4+2+2+3+4+5+6=27 = usual-care deaths in Table 2, confirming the count. Typographic percentage error; minor.

rows.R: Article: 134 unique messages (100 in month 1, 30 in month 2, 4 over months 3-6). This matches one plan document (p.80) but the protocol version headed V6.0 07.03.25 (p.16) says 178 messages with a different schedule, and another version (p.53) says 134 with an incompatible schedule. Which version governed delivery cannot be resolved.
rows.evidence: Supp1 PDF p.16, p.53, p.80 (rendered); main article PDF p.3 (text). Message log pp.101-109 not rendered.
rows.rationale: The compiled supplement contains several protocol versions with inconsistent dose descriptions; the version-dated V6.0 pages also carry the older 2,384/48-clinic design, so version labeling itself is unclear. The reported regimen agrees with the p.80 document. This is best described as version or timing ambiguity rather than a demonstrated deviation.

rows.R: Day-15 SOFA responders, precision immunotherapy: Table 2 52/131 (39.7%); Results text '39.7%; 51 of 131'. 52/131=39.7% and 51/131=38.9%, so the narrative numerator is the slip. Placebo 34/145 agrees.
